1.summary: Paul greets Titus, reminds him he was left in Crete to appoint elders in every town, lists the qualities of an elder, and warns against rebellious teachers, especially of the circumcision party, who ruin households for gain.
1.lookfor: Notice the qualities of an elder, and the hard words about Cretans.

names.name: Titus
names.gloss: A Greek co-worker of Paul, his true son in the faith.

names.name: Crete
names.gloss: A large island south of Greece.

insights.title: God who cannot lie
insights.body: Paul writes in hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before time began (1:2). On an island known for liars, God's truthfulness stands out.

insights.title: Titus
insights.body: Titus was a Greek whom Paul refused to have circumcised as a test case, and who later carried his hard letter to Corinth. Paul trusted him with difficult assignments.

insights.title: Elder and overseer
insights.body: Paul says to appoint elders (1:5), then describes the overseer (1:7). The two words describe the same leaders: elder speaks of maturity, overseer of their task.

insights.title: Hold fast and refute
insights.body: An elder must hold firmly to the faithful word, able both to encourage with sound teaching and to refute those who contradict it (1:9). Teaching builds up and guards.

insights.title: Cretans are always liars
insights.body: Paul quotes one of their own prophets: Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle gluttons (1:12). The line is usually attributed to Epimenides, a Cretan poet. To cretize was Greek slang for to lie.

insights.title: To the pure
insights.body: To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled nothing is pure (1:15). The false teachers' food and purity rules missed that defilement comes from the heart.

insights.title: Professing but denying
insights.body: They profess to know God, but deny him by their works (1:16). The theme of the letter: what we believe must show in how we live.

insights.title: Words and works
insights.body: Paul warns of people whose actions deny what they say. Where do your actions and beliefs not line up?

2.summary: Paul tells Titus to teach older men, older women, younger women, younger men and slaves how to live, so as to adorn the gospel, because God's grace has appeared, bringing salvation and training us to live godly lives as we wait for the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.
2.lookfor: Notice the purpose clauses ("so that...") and the two appearings in verses 11 and 13.

insights.title: Older women teaching
insights.body: Older women are to teach what is good and train the younger women (2:3-4). Discipling happens across generations.

insights.title: So the word isn't blasphemed
insights.body: Behavior is commended so that God's word isn't slandered (2:5), opponents have nothing bad to say (2:8), and the teaching of God is adorned (2:10). Ordinary faithfulness is a witness.

insights.title: Adorn
insights.body: Slaves are to adorn the doctrine of God our Savior in all things (2:10). The word kosmeō, from which comes cosmetics, means to make attractive. Even the lowest status could display the gospel's beauty.

insights.title: Grace that trains
insights.body: The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all, training us to renounce ungodliness and live sensibly, righteously and godly (2:11-12). Grace doesn't just forgive; it teaches.

insights.title: Epiphany
insights.body: The word appeared, epiphainō, was used of a god's manifestation or an emperor's arrival. Grace appeared in Jesus' first coming; we wait for the appearing of his glory (2:13).

insights.title: Our great God and Savior
insights.body: We wait for the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ (2:13), one of the clearest New Testament statements calling Jesus God.

insights.title: A people for his own possession
insights.body: He gave himself to redeem us and purify a people for his own possession, zealous for good works (2:14), echoing God's words to Israel at Sinai.

insights.title: Making it attractive
insights.body: Paul wants believers' lives to make the gospel beautiful. What in your life makes the faith attractive to others, or unattractive?

3.summary: Paul urges believers to be subject to rulers, ready for good works and gentle to all, remembering that they too were once foolish until God's kindness saved them by the washing of rebirth and renewal of the Spirit; he tells Titus to avoid foolish controversies, warn divisive people, and come to him at Nicopolis.
3.lookfor: Notice the before and after in verses 3 to 7, and the repeated emphasis on good works.

names.name: Artemas
names.gloss: A co-worker Paul might send to replace Titus.

names.name: Nicopolis
names.gloss: A city on the west coast of Greece, where Paul planned to winter.

insights.title: Gentle to all
insights.body: Speak evil of no one, be peaceable, gentle, showing every courtesy to everyone (3:2). Believers' manners toward outsiders matter.

insights.title: We too were once
insights.body: We ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, deceived, slaves to passions, hateful (3:3). Remembering our own past makes us gentle with others.

insights.title: Kindness and love for mankind
insights.body: When the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared (3:4). The word for love toward mankind is philanthrōpia, the root of philanthropy, a virtue rulers boasted of. God's is real.

insights.title: Not by works
insights.body: He saved us, not by works of righteousness we did, but according to his mercy, through the washing of rebirth and renewing by the Holy Spirit (3:5). A whole gospel in one sentence.

insights.title: Poured out richly
insights.body: The Spirit was poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ (3:6), as Joel foretold and Pentecost fulfilled.

insights.title: Winter at Nicopolis
insights.body: Paul plans to winter at Nicopolis (3:12). Sea travel stopped in winter, so plans were made around the seasons.

insights.title: Lacking nothing
insights.body: Help Zenas and Apollos on their journey, so they lack nothing (3:13). Supporting travelling workers was itself a good work.

insights.title: Remembering who you were
insights.body: Paul says we were once just as lost as anyone. How might remembering that change how you treat someone difficult this week?

intro.who: The letter names Paul, writing to Titus, a Gentile co-worker he had left on Crete (1:5). Like the letters to Timothy, some scholars attribute it to a later follower of Paul.
intro.when: If by Paul, about AD 62–64, between his imprisonments, perhaps from Macedonia; Paul planned to winter at Nicopolis (3:12).
intro.why: The new churches on Crete needed leaders, and false teachers were upsetting households. Paul tells Titus to appoint elders, silence troublemakers, and teach every group to live in a way that makes the gospel attractive, grounded in God's grace that saves and trains.

outline.title: Sound living for every age, shaped by grace
Good works and the kindness of God
